newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine interest rates to stay in double digits.
newsitem.headline: Philippine interest rates to stay in double digits.

text.p: The Philippines' 91-day Treasury bills yield was likely to stay in double digits in the second half of the year despite excess domestic liquidity in the system, money market traders said on Monday.

They said the monetary authority would not allow the repeat of the April incident when the bellwether 91-day T-bill rate slipped below 10 percent, narrowing its interest rate premium and prompting some foreign funds to shift their portfolio investments abroad.
"Definitely, we won't see rates going down to single digit again. I think the Central Bank has learned its lesson," the chief trader at a big foreign bank told Reuters.
The outflow was further exacerbated by the spillover from the Thai baht when foreign fund managers tagged the Philippines as the next Thailand.
The Central Bank had to raise its overnight borrowing rate to 20 percent to discourage the outflow. It has since lowered the rate to 13 percent after the foreign exchange market calmed down.

The traders' expectation was bolstered on Monday after the 91-day T-bill rate went up by 6.3 basis points to 10.356 percent despite excess liquidity in the system. It was the first uptick after three weeks of continuous decline.
"I don't think the rate will go down below 10 percent, because the Central Bank has been keeping its special series T-bill rate at 10.10 percent," another trader said.
"It's still a Central Bank-driven market. It is the Central Bank which sets the rates," he added.
Central Bank treasurer Sergio Edeza disagreed, saying the rates were market-driven.
"The rates are market-driven so we don't really know whether we have seen the bottom," Edeza told reporters after the auction.
He, however, said the Central Bank would assess the market before cutting its overnight and term rates later in the week.
Edeza also dismissed market talk the Central Bank was intensifying its mopping up operation, by hiking its dollar selling price.

On Friday, the Central Bank raised its dollar selling price to 26.385 pesos from 26.375, saying that it was just preparing for the usual weekend arbitrage play. It had lowered its benchmark rate to 26.377 on Monday.
This was for the second weekend in a row that the Central Bank raised its dollar selling rate.
"It will not be a regular thing," Edeza said, adding that the Central Bank can devise other ways to discourage arbitrageurs. He declined to say how.

Another trader, however, said the 91-day T-bill rate might slip below 10 percent, albeit briefly, in July after 6.5 billion pesos worth of fresh funds would be flushed out of the system due to the one percentage point reserve requirement cut.
"We might see that happening after three or four auctions. But still, it will be really depend on Central Bank," a trader a one foreign bank said.
